units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
Oh! I do that as it is. And self-sacrifice is a thing that should be put down by law. It is so demoralising to the people for whom one sacrifices oneself. They always go to the bad.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: As if anything could demoralise Robert Chiltern! You seem to forget that I know his real character.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: What you know about him is not his real character. It was an act of folly done in his youth, dishonourable, I admit, shameful, I admit, unworthy of him, I admit, and therefore . . . not his true character.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: How you men stand up for each other!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: How you women war against each other!
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Bitterly .
I only war against one woman, against Gertrude Chiltern. I hate her. I hate her now more than ever.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Because you have brought a real tragedy into her life, I suppose.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: With a sneer .
Oh, there is only one real tragedy in a woman’s life. The fact that her past is always her lover, and her future invariably her husband.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Lady Chiltern knows nothing of the kind of life to which you are alluding.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: A woman whose size in gloves is seven and three-quarters never knows much about anything. You know Gertrude has always worn seven and three-quarters? That is one of the reasons why there was never any moral sympathy between us. . . . Well, Arthur, I suppose this romantic interview may be regarded as at an end. You admit it was romantic, don’t you? For the privilege of being your wife I was ready to surrender a great prize, the climax of my diplomatic career. You decline. Very well. If Sir Robert doesn’t uphold my Argentine scheme, I expose him. Voilà tout .
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: You mustn’t do that. It would be vile, horrible, infamous.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Shrugging her shoulders .

Oh! don’t use big words. They mean so little. It is a commercial transaction. That is all. There is no good mixing up sentimentality in it. I offered to sell Robert Chiltern a certain thing. If he won’t pay me my price, he will have to pay the world a greater price. There is no more to be said. I must go. Good-bye. Won’t you shake hands?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: With you? No. Your transaction with Robert Chiltern may pass as a loathsome commercial transaction of a loathsome commercial age; but you seem to have forgotten that you came here to-night to talk of love, you whose lips desecrated the word love, you to whom the thing is a book closely sealed, went this afternoon to the house of one of the most noble and gentle women in the world to degrade her husband in her eyes, to try and kill her love for him, to put poison in her heart, and bitterness in her life, to break her idol, and, it may be, spoil her soul. That I cannot forgive you. That was horrible. For that there can be no forgiveness.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Arthur, you are unjust to me. Believe me, you are quite unjust to me. I didn’t go to taunt Gertrude at all. I had no idea of doing anything of the kind when I entered. I called with Lady Markby simply to ask whether an ornament, a jewel, that I lost somewhere last night, had been found at the Chilterns’. If you don’t believe me, you can ask Lady Markby. She will tell you it is true. The scene that occurred happened after Lady Markby had left, and was really forced on me by Gertrude’s rudeness and sneers. I called, oh!—a little out of malice if you like—but really to ask if a diamond brooch of mine had been found. That was the origin of the whole thing.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: A diamond snake-brooch with a ruby?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Yes. How do you know?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Because it is found. In point of fact, I found it myself, and stupidly forgot to tell the butler anything about it as I was leaving.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Goes over to the writing-table and pulls out the drawers .
It is in this drawer. No, that one. This is the brooch, isn’t it?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Holds up the brooch .
Yes. I am so glad to get it back. It was . . a present.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Won’t you wear it?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Certainly, if you pin it in.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: LORD GORING suddenly clasps it on her arm .
Why do you put it on as a bracelet? I never knew it could be worn as a bracelet.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Really?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Holding out her handsome arm .
No; but it looks very well on me as a bracelet, doesn’t it?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Yes; much better than when I saw it last.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: When did you see it last?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: Calmly .
Oh, ten years ago, on Lady Berkshire, from whom you stole it.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Starting .
What do you mean?
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: I mean that you stole that ornament from my cousin, Mary Berkshire, to whom I gave it when she was married. Suspicion fell on a wretched servant, who was sent away in disgrace. I recognised it last night. I determined to say nothing about it till I had found the thief. I have found the thief now, and I have heard her own confession.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Tossing her head .
It is not true.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: You know it is true. Why, thief is written across your face at this moment.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: I will deny the whole affair from beginning to end. I will say that I have never seen this wretched thing, that it was never in my possession.
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY

units.text: MRS. CHEVELEY tries to get the bracelet off her arm , but fails .
LORD GORING looks on amused .
Her thin fingers tear at the jewel to no purpose .
A curse breaks from her .

The drawback of stealing a thing, Mrs. Cheveley, is that one never knows how wonderful the thing that one steals is. You can’t get that bracelet off, unless you know where the spring is. And I see you don’t know where the spring is. It is rather difficult to find.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: You brute! You coward!
units.name: MRS. CHEVELEY
